title: Tables, Rows, Columns, Records and Fields
learningObjectives: Explain the core concepts of Tables, Rows, Columns, Records and Fields.
Identify the SQL structures and terminology used in this topic.
Read and interpret an original SQL example related to Tables, Rows, Columns, Records and Fields.
Predict the expected behaviour or result of a query in the stated engine context.
Apply safe and maintainable practices when using this concept.

understand.concept: A relational table represents data about one kind of entity or relationship. Each row contains one record, and each column describes an attribute shared by the rows. A table definition specifies column names and data types; constraints can add rules about permitted values.
understand.whyItMatters: Clear table structure makes data easier to query, validate and maintain. Choosing meaningful columns and consistent types also reduces ambiguity when applications exchange information with a database.
understand.analogy: A table resembles a spreadsheet: column headings describe attributes and each row contains one item's values.
understand.analogyLimit: A relational table is not simply a spreadsheet. It has defined types, constraints, keys and query semantics; row order is not guaranteed unless a query specifies ORDER BY.

explain.narrative:
## Table structure
Consider a Student table with student_id, full_name and email columns. Each row represents one student. A column has a name and a declared type or type affinity, depending on the database engine.

## Rows and columns
A row is also called a record or tuple in common teaching language. A column is also called a field or attribute. Each row should represent one consistent entity or relationship. Avoid storing several unrelated values in one column when they should be represented separately.

## Example schema
CREATE TABLE Student (student_id INTEGER, full_name TEXT, email TEXT);
This creates a table structure. It does not insert any student records. INSERT statements are used to add rows in a later lesson.

## Table order is not guaranteed
Without ORDER BY, a query result has no guaranteed row order. Even if rows appear in insertion order during a test, applications must not depend on that behaviour.

## Naming and design
Use clear, consistent names. Avoid ambiguous columns such as value or data when a more descriptive name is available. Choose data types and constraints based on the values and rules the application must store.

examples.title: Create a student table
examples.code: CREATE TABLE Student (student_id INTEGER, full_name TEXT, email TEXT);
examples.explanation: CREATE TABLE defines a table and its columns. This introductory schema intentionally adds keys and constraints in later lessons.

examples.title: Insert one sample row
examples.code: INSERT INTO Student (student_id, full_name, email) VALUES (1, 'Asha Rao', 'asha@example.test');
examples.explanation: INSERT adds one record. The .test domain is reserved for examples and is not a real contact address.

examples.title: Read the table columns
examples.explanation: The SELECT list chooses two columns; email is not included in the result.

examples.title: Count table records
examples.code: SELECT COUNT(*) AS student_count FROM Student;
examples.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows, including rows where some column values are NULL.

examples.title: Inspect a value with an alias
examples.code: SELECT email AS contact_address FROM Student;
examples.explanation: AS assigns a result-column alias. It does not rename the stored column.

practise.independentTask: Create a small relational database scenario that demonstrates Tables, Rows, Columns, Records and Fields. Write at least three queries or statements, explain the expected result, and identify any assumptions about the database dialect.

questions.prompt: What should a learner do when a query changes data?
options: Understand its target rows and constraints before execution
Run it repeatedly without checking
Remove every WHERE clause
Assume the operation can always be undone
questions.answer: Understand its target rows and constraints before execution
questions.explanation: Data-changing statements require careful scope and integrity checks.

questions.prompt: Which is a sound learning approach?
options: Predict the result, execute the query and explain the output
Memorize query text without understanding it
Treat NULL as zero in all cases
Assume a successful query proves the design is correct
questions.answer: Predict the result, execute the query and explain the output
questions.explanation: Prediction and verification build understanding and expose incorrect assumptions.
